results.point_context:
## Why They See Different Stakes

All three want the same thing: the right person in the right job. But the wager differs. The applicant risks losing a chance unseen; the recruiter risks speed without explanation; the owner risks the company’s future and responsibility. Their power is uneven: the applicant is judged, the recruiter runs a tool without choosing it, and the owner decides whether to use it. New York City’s yearly bias check and notice rule adds work for the recruiter, limits the owner’s choice, and leaves the applicant without control. One company stopped an internal tool after it rated women’s résumés lower. Outside rules and past failures mean these reasons cannot simply be added.

results.point_context:
### A Third Voice: Watching the Dashboard

I look at the weekly dashboard: how long hiring takes and what it costs. I need enough people, quickly enough, to keep the business moving. Other companies have reported hiring faster and spending less after using AI, so the choice can feel tied to survival. But when I see a tool facing a discrimination case, I think about my own name on the decision. I cannot hand that risk to a machine. I am protecting the company’s future and trust in my judgment.

results.point_context:
### Another Voice: At the Recruiter’s Desk

I open the screening tool after a morning of applications. It helps me sort résumés and match people with jobs. Then an applicant asks how the system was checked. I cannot answer, “The computer said so.” I may prepare a bias-check summary and explain the notice. One company has publicly shown this process under New York City law. I also judge AI-written applications: useful skill, or less effort? I did not choose the direction; I must use the tool and answer for it.
